I love bikes so much.

They’ve helped so many causes through the ages such as workers rights because they made it possible for people to live far from their workplace, giving their bosses far less power over them and allowing people to maintain strong family and community bonds. They also revolutionized women’s mobility and most feminist groups track their start back to the invention of the bike.

And seeing how much digital surveillance, such as flock cameras, is starting to shape what our governments and the police know about us maybe it’s time to get a bike if you don’t already have one?

I’m not under the illusion that everyone can just jump on a bike and be good to go, nor am I blind to the limitations of bikes, but they’re silent, they can go places bigger or heavier vehicles can’t, you never have to pay for parking, there’s no tax on them, no number plates, no one even needs to know you have one, there’s plenty of YouTube videos about how to repair them at home, and you can fit loads of baskets and saddle bags and whatnot on them if you need to transport stuff (or you can get a cargo bike that’s less mobile if you want to get fancy about it). You can even get foldable bikes that fit in a car.

What I’m trying to get at is, if you’re on your way to do something your government might not like (like a protest) and might need a quick silent getaway, bikes have always been the friends of the downtrodden, the powerless and revolutionaries.

[![Image 6: White-headed fruit dove](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8e/PtilopusEugeniaeKeulemans_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-PtilopusEugeniaeKeulemans_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:PtilopusEugeniaeKeulemans_(cropped).jpg "White-headed fruit dove")

The **[white-headed fruit dove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White-headed_fruit_dove "White-headed fruit dove")** (_Ptilinopus eugeniae_) is a species of bird in the pigeon family, [Columbidae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbidae "Columbidae"). It was [described](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Species_description "Species description") by [John Gould](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Gould "John Gould") in 1856, and the [specific name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Specific_name_(zoology) "Specific name (zoology)")_eugeniae_ honours [Eugénie de Montijo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eug%C3%A9nie_de_Montijo "Eugénie de Montijo"). Adults of the species have white heads, a purplish-red breast patch, a grey shoulder patch, olive-green [upperparts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_bird_terms#upperparts "Glossary of bird terms"), greenish [underparts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_bird_terms#underparts "Glossary of bird terms") with a blue tinge, and a yellowish [vent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_bird_terms#vent "Glossary of bird terms"). Juveniles have green heads with the white restricted to the forehead and upper throat, a much smaller grey shoulder patch, and the red breast patch restricted to the centre of the breast. The species is [endemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endemism "Endemism") to [Makira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Makira "Makira") and the nearby islands of [Ugi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ugi_Island "Ugi Island") and [Malaupaina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaupaina "Malaupaina") in the Solomon Islands. It inhabits lowland, hill, and ridge forest, along with neighbouring agricultural areas, and is especially common in [foothills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foothills "Foothills"). Its diet consists of small-seeded fruits and berries. The [IUCN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Union_for_Conservation_of_Nature "International Union for Conservation of Nature") considers it a [least-concern species](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Least-concern_species "Least-concern species"). Although it can adapt to [disturbed habitat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disturbance_(ecology) "Disturbance (ecology)"), it is threatened by [deforestation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deforestation "Deforestation") and [habitat loss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habitat_destruction "Habitat destruction"). _(**[Full article...](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White-headed\_fruit\_dove "White-headed fruit dove")**)_

**Ashley Brooke Moody** (born March 28, 1975) is an American politician and attorney serving since 2025 as the [junior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seniority_in_the_United_States_Senate "Seniority in the United States Senate")[United States senator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_senator "United States senator") from [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"). A member of the [Republican Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)"), she served from 2019 to 2025 as the 38th [attorney general of Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attorney_general_of_Florida "Attorney general of Florida").

Born in [Plant City, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plant_City,_Florida "Plant City, Florida"), Moody is an alumna of the [University of Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Florida "University of Florida") and [Stetson University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stetson_University "Stetson University"). She worked in civil litigation and then as an [assistant U.S. attorney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assistant_United_States_Attorney "Assistant United States Attorney") at the [U.S. Attorney's Office in the Middle District of Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Attorney_for_the_Middle_District_of_Florida "United States Attorney for the Middle District of Florida") until she was elected as a [circuit court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circuit_court_(Florida) "Circuit court (Florida)") judge in [Hillsborough County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillsborough_County,_Florida "Hillsborough County, Florida") in 2006. She remained in that role until 2017, when she [resigned to run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resign-to-run_law "Resign-to-run law") for Florida attorney general.

As Florida attorney general, Moody supported lawsuits to invalidate the [Affordable Care Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affordable_Care_Act "Affordable Care Act") and opposed the [legalization of recreational cannabis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legalization_of_non-medical_cannabis_in_the_United_States "Legalization of non-medical cannabis in the United States"). She supported President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") in [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida") during the [2020 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Florida "2020 United States presidential election in Florida"), and joined the lawsuit _[Texas v. Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas\_v.\_Pennsylvania "Texas v. Pennsylvania")_, which sought to [overturn the results of the election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attempts_to_overturn_the_2020_United_States_presidential_election "Attempts to overturn the 2020 United States presidential election").

In January 2025, Florida Governor [Ron DeSantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_DeSantis "Ron DeSantis") appointed Moody to the U.S. Senate seat vacated by the resignation of [Marco Rubio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Rubio "Marco Rubio"), who became [United States secretary of state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State") in the [Trump administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_presidency_of_Donald_Trump "Second presidency of Donald Trump"). Moody is the Republican nominee in the [2026 United States Senate special election in Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_United_States_Senate_special_election_in_Florida#Republican_primary "2026 United States Senate special election in Florida").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashley_Moody#cite_note-1)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ashley_Moody&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Moody was born in [Plant City, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plant_City,_Florida "Plant City, Florida"), on March 28, 1975.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashley_Moody#cite_note-family-2) She is the oldest of three children born to Carol and Judge [James S. Moody Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_S._Moody_Jr. "James S. Moody Jr.")[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashley_Moody#cite_note-herald-3)

Moody graduated from [Plant City High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plant_City_High_School "Plant City High School") in 1993.[[4]](

The **Florida attorney general** is the chief legal officer of the [U.S. state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._state "U.S. state") of [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"). The officeholder is a member of the [Florida Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Cabinet "Florida Cabinet") and the head of the state Department of Legal Affairs. The office is one of Florida's three elected state cabinet posts, along with the [chief financial officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_Financial_Officer_of_Florida "Chief Financial Officer of Florida") and [agriculture commissioner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Commissioner_of_Agriculture "Florida Commissioner of Agriculture").

*   Not be less than 30 years old;
*   Have resided in the state for the preceding 7 years; and

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Florida_Attorney_General&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Removal from office")]

*   Other duties incident or usual to the office; and

# Attorney General Rob Bonta

1.   [Home](https://oag.ca.gov/)
2.   Attorney General Rob Bonta

[![Image 4: Attorney General Rob Bonta](https://oag.ca.gov/sites/default/files/media/ag-bonta-official-2.jpg)Download high-resolution photo.](https://oag.ca.gov/sites/default/files/media/ag-bonta-official-2.jpg)
Rob Bonta is using his role as Attorney General of the State of California to make life better for everyone in the Golden State. Be it tackling crime, addressing the rising cost of living, or holding bad actors accountable when they harm Californians, Attorney General Bonta is committed to serving, protecting, and solving problems for the 39 million people who call California home.

Bonta’s passion for justice and service was passed on to him by his parents, who served on the frontlines of some of America's most important social justice movements. Instilling in him the lessons they learned from the United Farm Workers, the civil rights movement, and the People Power Revolution in the Philippines, Bonta's parents lit a fire inside him to stand up for those who are taken advantage of or hurt. It is why he decided to become an attorney — to help right historic wrongs, fight for vulnerable communities, and find real solutions that help everyday people.

Since becoming California’s 34 th Attorney General, Bonta has led California DOJ to take on some of the biggest challenges of our time — the lawlessness of the second Trump Administration, attacks on healthcare, deception peddled by Big Oil, and the state’s housing crisis. As California’s Chief Law Enforcement Officer, crime and public safety are Bonta’s top priorities, which is why he is at the helm of California DOJ’s work to crack down on fentanyl, dismantle organized retail crime schemes, remove illicit firearms from communities, fight for commonsense gun reforms, combat human trafficking, and address hate crimes. As the People’s Attorney, Bonta sees seeking accountability from those who abuse their power and take advantage of hardworking people as a critical component of the job. From protecting the rights of workers, tenants, and homeowners to taking on greedy corporate giants, wage theft, price gougers, and hidden fees, Bonta is standing up for consumers and making life more affordable for all Californians.

Before serving as Attorney General, Bonta spent more than eight years serving in the State Assembly, where he authored nation-leading legislation to make our communities safer and more affordable, and to ensure government institutions work for all of the people they serve. Some of his proudest achievements as a legislator include creating the strongest tenant protection law in the nation, ending surprise medical bills, strengthening voting rights, banning for-profit private prisons, and protecting immigrants and workers.

Prior to serving in the Assembly, Attorney General Bonta worked as a Deputy City Attorney for the City and County of San Francisco, where he represented the City and County and its workers, and fought to protect Californians from exploitation. Before that he worked in private practice, where he protected Californians from racial profiling.

Bonta was sworn in on April 23, 2021, becoming the first person of Filipino descent to serve as California Attorney General. Born in Quezon City, Philippines, Bonta immigrated to California with his family as an infant. He is the son of a proud native Filipina mother and a father born and raised in California. Bonta grew up and attended public school in California before working his way through Yale University and earning his Juris Doctor from Yale Law School. He is married to Mia Bonta, and they are the proud parents of three children, Reina, Iliana, and Andres; and adorable pup, Luna.

2.   Attorney General Rob Bonta

[![Image 4: Attorney General Rob Bonta](https://oag.ca.gov/sites/default/files/media/ag-bonta-official-2.jpg)Download high-resolution photo.](https://oag.ca.gov/sites/default/files/media/ag-bonta-official-2.jpg)
Rob Bonta is using his role as Attorney General of the State of California to make life better for everyone in the Golden State. Be it tackling crime, addressing the rising cost of living, or holding bad actors accountable when they harm Californians, Attorney General Bonta is committed to serving, protecting, and solving problems for the 39 million people who call California home.

Bonta’s passion for justice and service was passed on to him by his parents, who served on the frontlines of some of America's most important social justice movements. Instilling in him the lessons they learned from the United Farm Workers, the civil rights movement, and the People Power Revolution in the Philippines, Bonta's parents lit a fire inside him to stand up for those who are taken advantage of or hurt. It is why he decided to become an attorney — to help right historic wrongs, fight for vulnerable communities, and find real solutions that help everyday people.

Since becoming California’s 34 th Attorney General, Bonta has led California DOJ to take on some of the biggest challenges of our time — the lawlessness of the second Trump Administration, attacks on healthcare, deception peddled by Big Oil, and the state’s housing crisis. As California’s Chief Law Enforcement Officer, crime and public safety are Bonta’s top priorities, which is why he is at the helm of California DOJ’s work to crack down on fentanyl, dismantle organized retail crime schemes, remove illicit firearms from communities, fight for commonsense gun reforms, combat human trafficking, and address hate crimes. As the People’s Attorney, Bonta sees seeking accountability from those who abuse their power and take advantage of hardworking people as a critical component of the job. From protecting the rights of workers, tenants, and homeowners to taking on greedy corporate giants, wage theft, price gougers, and hidden fees, Bonta is standing up for consumers and making life more affordable for all Californians.

Before serving as Attorney General, Bonta spent more than eight years serving in the State Assembly, where he authored nation-leading legislation to make our communities safer and more affordable, and to ensure government institutions work for all of the people they serve. Some of his proudest achievements as a legislator include creating the strongest tenant protection law in the nation, ending surprise medical bills, strengthening voting rights, banning for-profit private prisons, and protecting immigrants and workers.

Prior to serving in the Assembly, Attorney General Bonta worked as a Deputy City Attorney for the City and County of San Francisco, where he represented the City and County and its workers, and fought to protect Californians from exploitation. Before that he worked in private practice, where he protected Californians from racial profiling.

Bonta was sworn in on April 23, 2021, becoming the first person of Filipino descent to serve as California Attorney General. Born in Quezon City, Philippines, Bonta immigrated to California with his family as an infant. He is the son of a proud native Filipina mother and a father born and raised in California. Bonta grew up and attended public school in California before working his way through Yale University and earning his Juris Doctor from Yale Law School. He is married to Mia Bonta, and they are the proud parents of three children, Reina, Iliana, and Andres; and adorable pup, Luna.

**Merrick Brian Garland** (born November 13, 1952) is an American lawyer and jurist who served as the 86th [United States attorney general](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_attorney_general "United States attorney general") from 2021 to 2025. He previously served as a [circuit judge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_federal_judge "United States federal judge") of the [United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Court_of_Appeals_for_the_District_of_Columbia_Circuit "United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit") from 1997 to 2021. In 2016, the [U.S. Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") refused to hold a confirmation hearing after President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama")[nominated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland_Supreme_Court_nomination "Merrick Garland Supreme Court nomination") him to the [U.S. Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States").

A native of the [Chicago area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_area "Chicago area"), Garland attended [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University") and [Harvard Law School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Law_School "Harvard Law School"), where he was an editor of the _[Harvard Law Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard\_Law\_Review "Harvard Law Review")_. He served as a [law clerk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_clerk "Law clerk") to Judge [Henry Friendly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Friendly "Henry Friendly") of the [United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Court_of_Appeals_for_the_Second_Circuit "United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit") and to [U.S. Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States") Justice [William J. Brennan Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_J._Brennan_Jr. "William J. Brennan Jr."), and then practiced corporate litigation at [Arnold & Porter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_&_Porter "Arnold & Porter"), after which he worked as a federal prosecutor in the [United States Department of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Justice "United States Department of Justice"), where he supervised the investigation and prosecution of the [Oklahoma City bombers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma_City_bombing "Oklahoma City bombing"). President [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") appointed Garland to the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit in 1997, and he served as its chief judge from 2013 to 2020.

President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama"), a [Democrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)"), [nominated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland_Supreme_Court_nomination "Merrick Garland Supreme Court nomination") Garland to serve as an [associate justice of the Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associate_Justice_of_the_Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States") in March 2016 to fill the vacancy created by the death of [Antonin Scalia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonin_Scalia "Antonin Scalia"). However, the [Republican Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_Republican_Conference "Senate Republican Conference")[majority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party_leaders_of_the_United_States_Senate "Party leaders of the United States Senate") refused to hold a hearing or vote on his nomination. The unprecedented refusal of a [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") majority to consider a Supreme Court nomination was highly controversial. Garland's nomination lasted 293 days (the longest to date), and it expired on January 3, 2017, at the end of the [114th Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/114th_Congress "114th Congress"). Eventually, subsequent President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump"), a [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)"), nominated [Neil Gorsuch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Gorsuch "Neil Gorsuch") to the vacant seat, and the Republican Senate majority confirmed him.

President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") nominated Garland as U.S. attorney general in January 2021. He was confirmed by the Senate in a 70–30 vote, and took office in March of that same year. During his tenure, Garland was criticized for the pace of the prosecution of President Donald Trump. Some observers, including Biden, assigned Garland some responsibility for the fact that none of the indictments obtained by special counsel [Jack Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Smith_(lawyer) "Jack Smith (lawyer)") went to trial before the [November 2024 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_presidential_election "2024 United States presidential election") in which Trump prevailed and won re-election to a second non-consecutive term leading to all charges against him being dismissed.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-Lemire_Politico-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-Khardori_politico-3)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Merrick_Garland&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Garland was born on November 13, 1952, in [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-4) His mother Shirley ([née](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_name#Maiden_and_married_names "Birth name")Horwitz; 1925–2016)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-5) was a director of volunteer services at [Chicago's Council for Jewish Elderly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CJE_SeniorLife "CJE SeniorLife") (now called CJE SeniorLife). His father, Cyril Garland (1915–2000),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-6) headed Garland Advertising, a small business run out of the family home.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-ReputationCollegiality-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-nytimesref-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-ForwardStory-9) Garland was raised in [Conservative Judaism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Judaism "Conservative Judaism"); the family name had been changed from _Garfinkel_ several generations earlier. His grandparents left the [Pale of Settlement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pale_of_Settlement "Pale of Settlement") in the western [Russian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Empire "Russian Empire") in the early 20th century, fleeing [antisemitic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antisemitism_in_the_Russian_Empire "Antisemitism in the Russian Empire")[pogroms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Jewish_pogroms_in_the_Russian_Empire "Anti-Jewish pogroms in the Russian Empire") in what is now Ukraine and Poland.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-ForwardStory-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-10) Two of his grandmother's siblings were later murdered in [the Holocaust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Holocaust "The Holocaust").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-11) He is a second cousin of [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") six-term [Iowa Governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_governors_of_Iowa "List of governors of Iowa") and former [US Ambassador to China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_States_to_China "List of ambassadors of the United States to China")[Terry Branstad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terry_Branstad "Terry Branstad").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-12)

Garland grew up in the north Chicago border suburb of [Lincolnwood.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincolnwood,_Illinois "Lincolnwood, Illinois")[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-SweetChicagoNative-13)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-ReputationCollegiality-7) He attended [Niles West High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niles_West_High_School "Niles West High School") in [Skokie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skokie,_Illinois "Skokie, Illinois"), Illinois, where he was president of the student council, acted in theatrical productions, and was a member of the debate team.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-NYT1-14) He graduated in 1970 as the class [valedictorian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valedictorian "Valedictorian").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-ReputationCollegiality-7)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-SweetChicagoNative-13) Garland was also a [Presidential Scholar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_Scholars_Program "Presidential Scholars Program") and [National Merit Scholar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Merit_Scholar "National Merit Scholar").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-16) He then studied [social studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_studies "Social studies") at [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-ReputationCollegiality-7)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-NPR2010ShortList-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-OfficialCongressionalDirectory-18) He initially wanted to become a physician, but soon decided to become a lawyer instead.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-NYT1-14) He allied himself with his future boss, [Jamie Gorelick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamie_Gorelick "Jamie Gorelick"), when he was elected the only freshman member of a campus-wide committee on which Gorelick also served.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-WashPo3/27-19) During his college summers Garland volunteered as a speechwriter to Congressman [Abner J. Mikva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abner_J._Mikva "Abner J. Mikva").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-WashPo3/27-19) After President [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter") appointed Mikva to the [D.C. Circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D.C._Circuit "D.C. Circuit"), Mikva would rely on Garland when hiring [law clerks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_clerk "Law clerk").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-NYT_3/27-20) At Harvard, Garland wrote news articles and [theater reviews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_criticism "Theatre criticism") for the _[Harvard Crimson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Harvard\_Crimson "The Harvard Crimson")_, and was a resident of [Quincy House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quincy_House_(Harvard) "Quincy House (Harvard)").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-RosenEllement-22) Garland wrote his 235-page honors thesis on industrial [mergers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mergers_and_acquisitions "Mergers and acquisitions") in Britain in the 1960s.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-WashPo3/27-19)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-23) Garland graduated from Harvard in 1974 with a [Bachelor of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") in social studies[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-24), [_summa cum laude_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_honors#United_States "Latin honors"), and was elected to [Phi Beta Kappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phi_Beta_Kappa "Phi Beta Kappa").

Garland then attended Harvard Law School,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-NPR2010ShortList-17) where he was a member of the _Harvard Law Review_. Garland ran for the presidency of the _Law Review_ but lost to [Susan Estrich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Estrich "Susan Estrich"), so he served as an articles editor instead.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-WashPo3/27-19)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-OfficialCongressionalDirectory-18) As an articles editor, Garland assigned himself to edit a submission by U.S. Supreme Court justice [William Brennan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_J._Brennan_Jr. "William J. Brennan Jr.") on the topic of the role of [state constitutions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_constitution_(United_States) "State constitution (United States)") in safeguarding [individual rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Individual_right "Individual right").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-WashPo3/27-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-NYT_3/27-20)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-Mauro-25) This correspondence with Brennan later contributed to his winning a clerkship with the justice.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-Mauro-25) Garland graduated from Harvard Law School in 1977 with a [Juris Doctor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juris_Doctor "Juris Doctor"), _magna cum laude_.

## Early career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Merrick_Garland&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early career")]

After graduating from law school, Garland spent two years as a judicial [law clerk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_clerk "Law clerk"), first for Judge [Henry Friendly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Friendly "Henry Friendly") of the [U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Court_of_Appeals_for_the_Second_Circuit "U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit") (New York City) from 1977 to 1978 and then for Justice [William J. Brennan Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_J._Brennan_Jr. "William J. Brennan Jr.") of the [U.S. Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Supreme_Court "U.S. Supreme Court") from 1978 to 1979.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-OfficialCongressionalDirectory-18) After his clerkships, Garland spent two years as a special assistant to U.S. attorney general [Benjamin Civiletti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Civiletti "Benjamin Civiletti").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-ReputationCollegiality-7)

After the [Carter administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carter_administration "Carter administration") ended in 1981, Garland entered private practice at the law firm [Arnold & Porter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_&_Porter "Arnold & Porter").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-ReputationCollegiality-7) Garland practiced mostly corporate litigation, and was made a partner in 1985.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-ReputationCollegiality-7) In _[Motor Vehicles Manufacturers Ass'n v. State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motor\_Vehicles\_Manufacturers\_Ass'n\_v.\_State\_Farm\_Mutual\_Automobile\_Insurance\_Co. "Motor Vehicles Manufacturers Ass'n v. State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co.")_ (1983) Garland acted as counsel to an insurance company suing to reinstate an unpopular [automatic seat belt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automatic_seat_belt "Automatic seat belt") mandate.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-HarvLRev-26) After winning the case in both the District of Columbia Circuit Court and the Supreme Court, Garland wrote an 87-page _Harvard Law Review_ article describing the way courts use a heightened "hard look" [standard of review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_of_review "Standard of review") and [scope of review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scope_of_review "Scope of review") when an agency chooses [deregulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deregulation "Deregulation"), with increasing focus on the fidelity of the agencies' actions to congressional intent.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-HarvLRev-26) In 1985–86, while at Arnold & Porter, Garland was a lecturer at [Harvard Law School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Law_School "Harvard Law School"), where he taught [antitrust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_antitrust_law "United States antitrust law") law.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-OfficialCongressionalDirectory-18)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-Goldstein2010PotentialNom-27) He also published an article in the _[Yale Law Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale\_Law\_Journal "Yale Law Journal")_ urging a broader application of [antitrust immunity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parker_immunity_doctrine "Parker immunity doctrine") to state and local governments.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-HarvLRev-26)

Desiring to return to public service and do more trial work, in 1989 Garland became an [assistant United States attorney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assistant_United_States_attorney "Assistant United States attorney") in the [U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Attorney's_Office_for_the_District_of_Columbia "U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia"). As a line prosecutor, Garland represented the government in criminal cases ranging from [drug trafficking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drug_trafficking "Drug trafficking") to complex [public corruption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_corruption "Public corruption") matters.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-ReputationCollegiality-7) Garland was one of the three principal prosecutors who handled the investigation into [Washington, D.C. Mayor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C._Mayor "Washington, D.C. Mayor")[Marion Barry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marion_Barry "Marion Barry")'s possession of cocaine.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-wapo.voting-28)

Garland then briefly returned to Arnold & Porter, working there from 1992 to 1993.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-WashPo3/27-19) In 1993, Garland joined the new [Clinton administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton_administration "Bill Clinton administration") as deputy assistant attorney general in the [Criminal Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Justice_Criminal_Division "United States Department of Justice Criminal Division") of the [United States Department of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Justice "United States Department of Justice").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-ReputationCollegiality-7) The following year, Deputy Attorney General [Jamie Gorelick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamie_Gorelick "Jamie Gorelick")–a key mentor of Garland's[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-29)–asked Garland to be her [principal associate deputy attorney general](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_Associate_Deputy_Attorney_General "Principal Associate Deputy Attorney General").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-ReputationCollegiality-7)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-30)

In that role, Garland's responsibilities included the supervision of high-profile [domestic-terrorism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domestic_terrorism_in_the_United_States "Domestic terrorism in the United States") cases, including the [Oklahoma City bombing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma_City_bombing "Oklahoma City bombing"), [Ted Kaczynski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Kaczynski "Ted Kaczynski") (also known as the "Unabomber"), and the [Atlanta Olympics bombings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centennial_Olympic_Park_bombing "Centennial Olympic Park bombing").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-ReputationCollegiality-7)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-31) Garland insisted on being sent to Oklahoma City in the aftermath of the attack, in order to examine the crime scene and oversee the investigation in preparation for the prosecution.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-Savage-32) He represented the government at the [preliminary hearings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preliminary_hearing "Preliminary hearing") of the two main defendants, [Timothy McVeigh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_McVeigh "Timothy McVeigh") and [Terry Nichols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terry_Nichols "Terry Nichols").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-Savage-32) Garland offered to lead the trial team, but could not because he was needed at the [Justice Department headquarters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_F._Kennedy_Building "Robert F. Kennedy Building"). Instead, he helped pick the team and supervised it from Washington, D.C., where he was involved in major decisions, including the choice to seek the [death penalty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_punishment_in_the_United_States "Capital punishment in the United States") for McVeigh and Nichols.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-Savage-32) Garland won praise for his work on the case from the Republican [governor of Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Oklahoma "Governor of Oklahoma"), [Frank Keating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Keating "Frank Keating").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-ReputationCollegiality-7)

Garland served as co-chair of the administrative law section of the [District of Columbia Bar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/District_of_Columbia_Bar "District of Columbia Bar") from 1991 to 1994.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-OfficialCongressionalDirectory-18)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-33) He is also a member of the [American Law Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Law_Institute "American Law Institute").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-OfficialCongressionalDirectory-18)

In 2003, Garland was elected to the [Harvard Board of Overseers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Board_of_Overseers "Harvard Board of Overseers"), completing the unexpired term of [Deval Patrick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deval_Patrick "Deval Patrick"), who had stepped down from the board.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-34) Garland served as president of the overseers for 2009–10.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-35)

## Federal judicial service (1997–2021)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Merrick_Garland&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Federal judicial service (1997–2021)")]

### Appointment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Merrick_Garland&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Appointment")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f9/Merrick_Garland.jpg/250px-Merrick_Garland.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Merrick_Garland.jpg)

Garland in 2016 as chief judge of the [U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Court_of_Appeals_for_the_District_of_Columbia_Circuit "United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit")

On September 6, 1995, President [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") nominated Garland to the [U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Court_of_Appeals_for_the_District_of_Columbia "United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia") seat vacated by his longtime mentor [Abner J. Mikva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abner_J._Mikva "Abner J. Mikva").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-WashPo3/27-19) Justice Brennan, for whom Garland had clerked, recommended Garland for the position in a letter to Clinton.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-Mauro-25) The [American Bar Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Bar_Association "American Bar Association") (ABA) [Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standing_Committee_on_the_Federal_Judiciary "Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary") unanimously gave Garland a "well-qualified" committee rating, its highest.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-36)

On December 1, 1995, Garland received a hearing regarding the nomination before the [Senate Judiciary Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Judiciary_Committee "United States Senate Judiciary Committee").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-37) In Senate confirmation hearings Garland said that the Supreme Court justices whom he most admired were Justice Brennan, for whom he clerked, and [Chief Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_Justice_of_the_United_States "Chief Justice of the United States")[John Marshall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Marshall "John Marshall"). Garland also expressed admiration for the writing style of Justice [Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Wendell_Holmes_Jr. "Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr.")[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-38) However, Senate Republicans did not schedule a vote on Garland's confirmation,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-ReputationCollegiality-7) not because of concerns over Garland's qualifications, but because of a dispute over whether to fill the seat.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-Goldstein2010PotentialNom-27)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-:0-39)

After winning the November 1996 presidential election, Clinton renominated Garland on January 7, 1997.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-40) He was confirmed on March 19, 1997, by a 76–23 vote.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-41) The majority of Republican senators voted to confirm Garland, including senators [John McCain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McCain "John McCain"), [Orrin Hatch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orrin_Hatch "Orrin Hatch"), [Susan Collins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Collins_(politician) "Susan Collins (politician)"), and [Jim Inhofe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Inhofe "Jim Inhofe").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-PoliticoWheaton-42) Senators [Mitch McConnell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitch_McConnell "Mitch McConnell"), [Chuck Grassley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Grassley "Chuck Grassley"), and [Jeff Sessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Sessions "Jeff Sessions") were among those who voted against Garland.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-PoliticoWheaton-42) All of the 23 "no" votes came from Republicans, and all were said to be based "on whether there was even a need for an eleventh seat" on the D.C. Circuit.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-43) He received his judicial commission on March 20, 1997.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-fjc.gov-44)

### Service as chief judge of the D.C. Circuit

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Merrick_Garland&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Service as chief judge of the D.C. Circuit")]

Garland became chief judge of the D.C. Circuit on February 12, 2013.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-45) In May 2013 he announced that the D.C. Circuit had unanimously decided to provide the public with same-day audio recordings of [oral arguments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oral_argument "Oral argument") in the court.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-RCFPMediaLaw-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-47)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-fjc.gov-44) During his term, he was an active member of the [Judicial Conference of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judicial_Conference_of_the_United_States "Judicial Conference of the United States"),[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-PassesGavel-48) and was involved in the formulation of new rules to protect federal judicial branch employees from workplace harassment, which were adopted in the wake of multiple sexual misconduct allegations against Judge [Alex Kozinski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Kozinski "Alex Kozinski").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-PassesGavel-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-49) Garland's seven-year term as chief judge ended on February 11, 2020, with Judge [Sri Srinivasan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sri_Srinivasan "Sri Srinivasan") succeeding him.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-PassesGavel-48) Garland continued to serve as an active member of the court until his retirement.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-50)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-51)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-fjc.gov-44)

### Notable cases

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Merrick_Garland&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Notable cases")]

Garland is considered a judicial moderate and a [centrist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centrism "Centrism").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-ShearHarris-52) Garland has been described by [Nina Totenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nina_Totenberg "Nina Totenberg") and Carrie Johnson of [NPR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NPR "NPR") as "a moderate liberal, with a definite pro-prosecution bent in criminal cases".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-ReputationCollegiality-7)[Tom Goldstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Goldstein "Tom Goldstein"), the publisher of _[SCOTUSblog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SCOTUSblog "SCOTUSblog")_, wrote in 2010 that "Judge Garland's record demonstrates that he is essentially the model, neutral judge. His opinions avoid unnecessary, sweeping pronouncements."[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-Goldstein2010PotentialNom-27) Garland has a reputation for collegiality and his opinions rarely draw a dissent.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-BNA-53) As of 2016, Garland had written just fifteen dissents in his two decades on the court, fewer than his colleague [Brett Kavanaugh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brett_Kavanaugh "Brett Kavanaugh"), who wrote some 17 dissents over the previous decade.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-BNA-53)

#### Administrative and environmental law

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Merrick_Garland&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Administrative and environmental law")]

Garland has tended to favor deference to regulatory agencies.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-54) For example, in _In re Aiken County_ (2013), Garland dissented when the court issued [mandamus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandamus "Mandamus") ordering the [Nuclear Regulatory Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_Regulatory_Commission "Nuclear Regulatory Commission") to process the [Yucca Mountain nuclear waste repository](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yucca_Mountain_nuclear_waste_repository "Yucca Mountain nuclear waste repository") license.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-55) In _[Americans for Safe Access v. Drug Enforcement Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americans\_for\_Safe\_Access\_v.\_Drug\_Enforcement\_Administration "Americans for Safe Access v. Drug Enforcement Administration")_ (2013), Garland joined a divided court upholding the [DEA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drug_Enforcement_Administration "Drug Enforcement Administration")'s [classification of marijuana as a Schedule I drug](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Removal_of_cannabis_from_Schedule_I_of_the_Controlled_Substances_Act "Removal of cannabis from Schedule I of the Controlled Substances Act").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-NYT1-14) However, according to Goldstein, in a number of split decisions on [environmental law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_law "Environmental law") Garland "favored contested EPA regulations and actions when challenged by industry, and in other cases he has accepted challenges brought by [environmental groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmentalism "Environmentalism")."[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-Goldstein2010PotentialNom-27) In _Rancho Viejo, LLC v. Norton_ (2003), Garland found the [arroyo toad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arroyo_toad "Arroyo toad") was protected by the federal [Endangered Species Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endangered_Species_Act "Endangered Species Act").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-56) Circuit Judge [John Roberts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Roberts "John Roberts") dissented from the denial of rehearing [en banc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/En_banc "En banc"), writing that Congress's [interstate commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_commerce "Interstate commerce") power cannot reach "a hapless toad that, for reasons of its own, lives its entire life in California."[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-57)

#### Criminal law and whistleblower protection

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Merrick_Garland&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Criminal law and whistleblower protection")]

While on the [bench](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bench_(law) "Bench (law)"), Garland has shown a tendency to be deferential to the government in criminal cases, siding with prosecutors in ten of the fourteen criminal cases in which he disagreed with a colleague.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-NYTcriminal-58) For example, in _United States v. Watson_ (1999), Garland dissented when the court concluded a prosecutor's closing argument was unduly [prejudicial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmless_error "Harmless error"), objecting that a conviction should be reversed for only "the most egregious of these kind of errors."[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-NYTcriminal-58) In 2007, Garland dissented when the [en banc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/En_banc "En banc") D.C. Circuit reversed the conviction of a [Washington, D.C. police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Police_Department_of_the_District_of_Columbia "Metropolitan Police Department of the District of Columbia") officer who had accepted bribes in an FBI sting operation.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-WashPo3/18-59)

Garland has taken a broad view of [whistleblower protection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whistleblower_protection_in_the_United_States "Whistleblower protection in the United States") laws, such as the [False Claims Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/False_Claims_Act "False Claims Act") (FCA),[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-LoughranSwann-60) which creates a private cause of action against those [defrauding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fraud "Fraud") the federal government.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-WashPo3/18-59) For example, in _United States ex rel. Yesudian v. Howard University_ (1998), Garland wrote for the court in holding that a plaintiff alleging he had been fired by [Howard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_University "Howard University") for whistleblowing could sue under the FCA for retaliation.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-Goldstein2010PotentialNom-27) In _United States ex rel. Totten v. Bombardier Corp._ (2004), Garland dissented when the court, in an opinion written by Judge John Roberts, held that the FCA did not apply to false claims submitted to Amtrak because Amtrak is not the government.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-WashPo3/18-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-LoughranSwann-60) Roberts justified his narrow reading by citing a book by circuit judge [Henry Friendly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Friendly "Henry Friendly").[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-61) In dissent, Garland (who like Roberts had clerked for Friendly), cited Friendly's book as supporting the use of [legislative intent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legislative_intent "Legislative intent"),[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-WashPo3/18-59) writing that Roberts was relying on "'canons' of [statutory construction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statutory_construction "Statutory construction"), which serve there as 'cannons' of statutory destruction."[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-LoughranSwann-60)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-62) Garland's dissent, expressing concerns that the court's ruling would impede the government's ability to pursue false claims cases against federal grantees, is credited with sparking the [Fraud Enforcement and Recovery Act of 2009](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fraud_Enforcement_and_Recovery_Act_of_2009 "Fraud Enforcement and Recovery Act of 2009"), which eliminated the loophole.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-LoughranSwann-60) During confirmation hearings in 2005, Senator Chuck Grassley sharply questioned Roberts on why he had not adopted Garland's reading.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-WashPo3/18-59) Roberts replied, "Any time Judge Garland disagrees, you know you're in a difficult area."[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-WashPo3/18-59)

#### National security

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Merrick_Garland&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: National security")]

During Garland's tenure, the D.C. Circuit reviewed cases arising from the [Guantanamo Bay detention camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guantanamo_Bay_detention_camp "Guantanamo Bay detention camp"). In _[al Odah v. United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al\_Odah\_v.\_United\_States "Al Odah v. United States")_ (2003), a panel that included Garland unanimously held that federal courts could not hear challenges from Guantanamo detainees.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-Goldstein2010PotentialNom-27) In July 2011, Garland wrote for the unanimous panel when it rejected Guantanamo detainee [Moath Hamza Ahmed al Alawi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moath_Hamza_Ahmed_al_Alawi "Moath Hamza Ahmed al Alawi")'s petition for _[habeas corpus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habeas\_corpus "Habeas corpus")_.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-64) In _[Parhat v. Gates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parhat\_v.\_Gates "Parhat v. Gates")_ (2008), Garland wrote for a panel that unanimously overturned the [Combatant Status Review Tribunal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combatant_Status_Review_Tribunal "Combatant Status Review Tribunal")'s determination that a [captured Uyghur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uyghur_detainees_at_Guantanamo_Bay "Uyghur detainees at Guantanamo Bay") was an [enemy combatant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enemy_combatant "Enemy combatant").[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-NewYorkTimes20080624-65) In _Saleh v. Titan Corp._ (2009), Garland dissented from the court's holding that former Iraqi detainees at [Abu Ghraib prison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Ghraib_prison "Abu Ghraib prison") could not sue [private military contractors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_military_contractor "Private military contractor") who participated in [torture and prisoner abuse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Ghraib_torture_and_prisoner_abuse "Abu Ghraib torture and prisoner abuse"). Garland wrote that the suit should be allowed to proceed because "no act of Congress and no judicial precedent" immunized the contractors from [tort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tort "Tort") liability, the [Federal Tort Claims Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Tort_Claims_Act "Federal Tort Claims Act") specifically excludes contractors, and tort liability would not interfere with government operations.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-66)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-67)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-NYTCloseLook-68)

#### First Amendment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Merrick_Garland&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: First Amendment")]

According to Goldstein, Garland has "tended to take a broader view" of [First Amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution "First Amendment to the United States Constitution") rights.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-Goldstein2010PotentialNom-27) In cases involving the [Freedom of Information Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_Information_Act_(United_States) "Freedom of Information Act (United States)") and similar provisions related to [government transparency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_transparency "Government transparency"), "Judge Garland's rulings reflect a preference for open government."[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-Goldstein2010PotentialNom-27) In _ACLU v. CIA_ (2013), Garland wrote for a panel unanimously rejecting the agency's [Glomar response](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glomar_response "Glomar response") and ordering it to process the ACLU's FOIA request regarding [targeted killings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Targeted_killing "Targeted killing") by CIA drones.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-rcfp-69) In _Cause of Action v. FTC_ (2015), Garland wrote for a panel unanimously overturning the agency's limitation on FOIA fee waivers to large [news outlets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/News_media "News media").[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-rcfp-69)

In _Lee v. Department of Justice_ (2005), Garland dissented from the denial of rehearing en banc after the D.C. Circuit affirmed the [district court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_District_Court_for_the_District_of_Columbia "United States District Court for the District of Columbia")'s order holding reporters in [contempt of court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contempt_of_court "Contempt of court") for [refusing to testify](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reporter's_privilege "Reporter's privilege") about their [anonymous sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anonymous_source "Anonymous source") during the [Wen Ho Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wen_Ho_Lee "Wen Ho Lee") investigation.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-NYTCloseLook-68)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-AlmanancFedJudiciary-70) Garland wrote that the panel had erred in failing to "[weigh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balancing_test "Balancing test") the public interest in protecting the reporter's sources against the private interest in compelling disclosure" and that the decision "undermined the Founders' intention to protect the press 'so that it could bare the secrets of government and inform the people.'"[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-AlmanancFedJudiciary-70) In _Initiative & Referendum Institute v. U.S. Postal Service_ (2005), Garland wrote for the court, holding that a [U.S. Postal Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Postal_Service "United States Postal Service") regulation banning signature-gathering for [petitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petition "Petition") at post offices violated the First Amendment.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-Goldstein2010PotentialNom-27)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-AlmanancFedJudiciary-70) Garland found the regulation to be [facially](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facial_challenge "Facial challenge") overbroad and not [narrowly tailored](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narrow_tailoring "Narrow tailoring").[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-AlmanancFedJudiciary-70)

In cases involving [campaign finance reform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campaign_finance_reform_in_the_United_States "Campaign finance reform in the United States") laws, Garland has applied _[Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citizens\_United\_v.\_Federal\_Election\_Commission "Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission")_ when he believed that he was compelled to do so, but he has not sought to extend its holding.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-NYTCloseLook-68) In _Wagner v. Federal Election Commission_ (2015), Garland wrote for the unanimous en banc D.C. Circuit in upholding a prohibition on campaign contributions from [federal contractors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_contractor "Federal contractor") because of the governmental interest in preventing [corruption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_corruption "Political corruption").[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-NYTCloseLook-68)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-HasenElectionLaw-71) In _[National Association of Manufacturers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National\_Association\_of\_Manufacturers "National Association of Manufacturers") v. Taylor_ (2009), Garland wrote for the court in a decision upholding the constitutionality of [lobbyist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lobbyist "Lobbyist") disclosure requirements under the [Honest Leadership and Open Government Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honest_Leadership_and_Open_Government_Act "Honest Leadership and Open Government Act").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-RCFPMediaLaw-46)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-HasenElectionLaw-71) Professor [Rick Hasen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_L._Hasen "Richard L. Hasen"), an election-law expert, writes that Garland's opinions on election law are characterized by careful application of precedent and indicate that Garland believes in reasonable regulation.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-HasenElectionLaw-71)

Garland has addressed a number of [religious freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religious_freedom "Religious freedom") cases while on the D.C. Circuit, although several of these have been decided on procedural grounds.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-ReligiousFreedom-72) In 2002, Garland joined a unanimous court in ruling for two federal prisoners who were denied the right to consume [communion wine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communion_wine "Communion wine").[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-ReligiousFreedom-72)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-73) In 2010, Garland wrote the decision for a unanimous court in favor of an Interior Department employee who brought a religious-discrimination claim after the Interior Department refused to allow her to work weekdays rather than Sunday, when she wished to attend church and [Bible study](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bible_study_(Christian) "Bible study (Christian)").[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-ReligiousFreedom-72)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Garland#cite_note-74)

#### Second Amendment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Merrick_Garland&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Second Amendment")]

District of Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/District\_of\_Columbia\_v.\_Heller "District of Columbia v. Heller")_ invalidating the [D.C. handgun ban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gun_laws_in_the_District_of_Columbia "Gun laws in the District of Columbia").
